final_note: You worked through Electromagnetic waves: Visible light (physics only) — 9 specification statements.

concepts.def: The range of electromagnetic waves the human eye can detect, running from red at the long-wavelength end to violet at the short-wavelength end. The colours run continuously into one another rather than being separated by gaps.

concepts.term: Narrow band of wavelength and frequency
concepts.def: Each colour in the visible spectrum occupies a small range of wavelengths and a matching small range of frequencies, not a single value. Red occupies the longest-wavelength, lowest-frequency band; violet the shortest-wavelength, highest-frequency band.
Reflection from a smooth surface in a single direction. Parallel rays arriving at the surface stay parallel after reflection, so a clear image is formed, as in a plane mirror.

Reflection from a rough surface, which causes scattering. Each individual ray still obeys the law of reflection, but the surface normals point in many directions, so the reflected rays leave in many directions and no image is formed.
The spreading of reflected light into many directions, caused here by the unevenness of a rough surface. Scattering is why a sheet of paper looks equally bright from almost any viewing angle.

A material that absorbs certain wavelengths (and colours) of the light falling on it and transmits the other wavelengths (and colours). A filter removes light; it never adds light of a colour that was not already present.
The passing of light through a material, rather than the light being reflected from it or absorbed by it. Transmitted light emerges on the far side of the material.
The taking in of light energy by a material, so that the light does not leave the material as light. Wavelengths that are absorbed by an object are not available to be reflected or transmitted.
The fact that a single object treats different wavelengths differently, reflecting some strongly while absorbing others. This unequal treatment of the wavelengths is what gives an object its colour.
An object that transmits no light. Light falling on it is either reflected or absorbed, and its colour is set by the wavelengths it reflects most strongly.
A surface appears white when all wavelengths are reflected equally, and black when all wavelengths are absorbed. Black is therefore the absence of reflected light rather than a reflected colour.
Describes an object that transmits light without scattering it, so a clear image can be seen through it. Window glass and clear plastic are transparent.
Describes an object that transmits light but scatters it on the way through, so light gets through but no clear image can be seen. Frosted glass, tracing paper and thin fabric are translucent.

concepts.term: Colour of an object under coloured light
concepts.def: An object can only reflect wavelengths that are present in the light falling on it. If the illuminating light contains none of the wavelengths the object reflects, the object appears black.

mcqs.q: Which statement best describes the colours of the visible light spectrum?
options: Each colour has its own narrow band of wavelength and frequency
Each colour has one exact wavelength and one exact frequency
Each colour has its own wavelength but all share one frequency
All the colours share a wavelength band but differ in speed
mcqs.explain: This is the specification statement: every colour occupies a small range of wavelengths together with a matching small range of frequencies.

mcqs.q: Red light and violet light both lie within the visible spectrum. Which statement about their bands is correct?
options: The red band lies at one fixed wavelength and the violet at another
The red band has longer wavelengths, so it has lower frequencies
The red band has longer wavelengths but the same frequency
The red and violet bands cover the same range of wavelength
mcqs.explain: Each colour holds its own band of wavelength and of frequency; red sits at the long-wavelength, low-frequency end of the visible spectrum.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between specular reflection and diffuse reflection?
options: Specular reflection is from a rough surface, and diffuse from a smooth one
Specular reflection always obeys the law of reflection and diffuse does not
Specular reflection is from a smooth surface, diffuse from a rough one
Specular reflection sends light back and diffuse takes most of it in
mcqs.explain: The specification defines specular reflection as reflection from a smooth surface in a single direction, and diffuse reflection as reflection from a rough surface, which scatters the light.

mcqs.q: A mirror shows a clear image of a lamp, but a sheet of white paper beside it looks equally bright from every direction. Why does the paper behave differently?
options: Its rough surface obeys no law, so the rays leave at random angles
Its rough surface takes in the light and gives it out slowly
Its rough surface transmits light while the mirror reflects it
Its rough surface scatters light into many directions
mcqs.explain: Reflection from a rough surface causes scattering — diffuse reflection — so light leaves towards every viewing position and no image is formed.

mcqs.q: How does a colour filter work?
options: It reflects the unwanted wavelengths and lets the rest through
It absorbs certain wavelengths of light and transmits the others
It adds its own colour to the white light that passes through
It changes the wavelength of the light passing through it
mcqs.explain: This is the specification statement: filters work by absorbing certain wavelengths and colours, and transmitting the other wavelengths and colours.

mcqs.q: White light is shone through a blue filter. What emerges from the filter, and why?
options: All the colours, but with the blue much brighter than the rest
White light that has been dyed blue as it travelled through
Blue light, because the other wavelengths are absorbed by it
Blue light, because the other colours reflect back off it
mcqs.explain: White light contains every wavelength; the blue filter absorbs all of them except the blue band, which it transmits.

mcqs.q: What determines the colour of an opaque object viewed in white light?
options: The wavelengths that the object absorbs most strongly of all
The wavelengths that the object gives out when it is warm
The wavelengths that the object lets through itself
The wavelengths that the object reflects most strongly
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the colour of an opaque object is determined by which wavelengths are more strongly reflected; the rest are absorbed.

mcqs.q: A jumper appears white when it is lit by white light. What is happening to the light that falls on it?
options: All wavelengths are reflected equally
All wavelengths are absorbed equally by it
All wavelengths pass straight through the wool
Only the wavelengths of white are reflected
mcqs.explain: The specification states that if all wavelengths are reflected equally the object appears white.

mcqs.q: A piece of card looks black in a brightly lit room. Which explanation is correct?
options: The light passes straight through the card without stopping
The card reflects every wavelength that falls upon it equally
The card absorbs all of the wavelengths of light that fall on it
The card gives out no light of its own in the lit room
mcqs.explain: The specification states that if all wavelengths are absorbed the object appears black, because almost no light is reflected to the eye.

mcqs.q: Which statement is true of objects that transmit light?
options: They must be colourless as well as see-through
They transmit light only when very smooth
They are either translucent or opaque
They are either transparent or translucent
mcqs.explain: This is the specification statement: objects that transmit light are either transparent or translucent.

mcqs.q: Frosted bathroom glass lets light into the room, but no clear image can be seen through it. How is the glass best described?
options: Translucent, since it scatters the light passing through
Transparent, since the light gets through the glass easily
Opaque, since there is no clear image to be seen through it
Specular, since the rough surface reflects light
mcqs.explain: Light is transmitted, so the glass is not opaque, but the scattering destroys the image — which is exactly what translucent means.

mcqs.q: A book cover appears red in white light. Which explanation of its colour is correct?
options: Red is absorbed by the cover and other wavelengths reflected
Red is reflected and the other wavelengths absorbed
Red is transmitted through the cover and the rest reflected
Red light is given out by the cover in any conditions
mcqs.explain: Differential treatment of the wavelengths gives the colour: the red band is reflected most strongly and the wavelengths not reflected are absorbed.

mcqs.q: In white light a leaf looks green and a daisy petal looks white. Which explanation accounts for both?
options: The leaf absorbs green strongly and reflects the other wavelengths; the petal absorbs the whole range
The leaf reflects green and absorbs the others; the petal absorbs every wavelength equally
The leaf transmits green light through itself, and the petal transmits the whole range of light
The leaf reflects green strongly and absorbs the other wavelengths; the petal reflects them all equally
mcqs.explain: Colour comes from differential reflection and absorption: unequal reflection gives green, and equal reflection of every wavelength gives white.

mcqs.q: A red counter is viewed through a green filter in white light. How does the counter appear?
options: Black, because the filter absorbs the red light it reflects
Green, because the filter turns the light green as it passes
Red, because the reflected light still gets through it
Yellow, because red and green mix inside the filter
mcqs.explain: The counter reflects only red; the green filter absorbs red, so no light reaches the eye and the counter looks black.

mcqs.q: White light is passed through a red filter and then through a blue filter. What is seen after the second filter?
options: White light, because the second filter cancels the first out
Almost no light: each filter absorbs what the other passes
Purple light, because the red and the blue light add together
Blue light, since the second filter dyes the light blue
mcqs.explain: The red filter transmits only red and absorbs the rest; the blue filter then absorbs that red, so virtually nothing emerges.

mcqs.q: A blue mug is placed in a darkroom lit only by red light. How does the mug appear?
options: Purple, since the red light mixes with the mug's own blue
Blue, since the mug keeps its colour in any lighting
Black, as there is no blue light for it to reflect
Red, since the mug absorbs the red light and shows it
mcqs.explain: A blue object reflects blue and absorbs other wavelengths; with only red light present the red is absorbed and no light is reflected.
